lessons.title: What to think about during every rep
lessons.summary: Set up before you move. During the rep, use a simple cue. Afterwards, check your control and effort before changing the weight.

blocks.text: After this lesson, you can use a short before-during-after checklist on any exercise. Set up before moving, follow one useful cue during the rep, then judge whether the load and technique matched the plan.

A [[rep|repetition]] is a complete exercise movement. A [[set]] is a group of repetitions. Before the set, read the exercise guide and make your position repeatable. Adjust the machine, choose your grip and foot position, and check that the weight can be returned safely. Set safety supports when needed.

blocks.title: THIS Is Optimal Technique For Muscle Growth
blocks.why: Watch: Jeff Nippard explains how repeatable technique supports effective training.

groups.title: Before the set
items: Read the guide; adjust seat, grip and feet.
Check the load, clear space and safe stopping setup.
Choose your range and a simple movement cue.
Prepare your breathing and gently brace.

groups.title: During the set
items: Follow the planned path; keep your support steady.
Use the comfortable range you chose.
Control the lowering; lift without throwing the load.
Keep breathing appropriate to the effort.
Stop if pain or loss of control appears.

groups.title: After the set
items: Return the weight safely before checking your phone.
Log repetitions, weight and estimated clean reps left.
Note the cue that helped; rest before trying again.

blocks.caption: Tick these before training, not while holding a weight. Ticks stay on this device. Use Reset when you want a fresh checklist.

items.title: Set your starting position
items.text: For a light seated machine press, adjust the seat using its guide. Plant your feet and take the handles without shrugging.

items.title: Prepare to move
items.text: Gently tighten your middle: this is a [[brace]]. Breathe in before starting. Use the cue ‘push the handles away’.

items.title: Lift along the planned path
items.text: Press smoothly and breathe out as you push. Keep your back supported rather than chasing extra distance with your whole body.

items.title: Return with control
items.text: Guide the handles back through your comfortable [[range of motion]]. Do not let the stack crash or force a painful stretch.

items.title: Decide whether to repeat
items.text: If you can repeat the same movement, continue within your plan. Otherwise return the load safely and end the set.

blocks.text: The exact path depends on the exercise; there is no universal ‘elbows here’ rule. During a heavy or unfamiliar move, an outcome cue can be easier than naming every muscle. See [[lesson:tech-mind-muscle|how to choose a focus cue]]. Learn the details with light practice before adding demanding weight.

left.title: Do ✓
items: Choose a cue you can actually follow while moving.
Keep the movement repeatable as effort rises.
Use [[reps in reserve]] to describe clean repetitions left.

right.title: Avoid ✕
items: Changing every detail of your technique at once.
Shortening the movement just to finish the number.
Counting imagined repetitions that need a big body swing.

blocks.text: After the set, ask what limited you: the working muscles, your grip, breathlessness, or losing the position? Write a brief note in LiftLog. That helps you choose the next load without turning technique into a perfection contest. [[lesson:tech-choosing-weight|Choosing weight]] handles that decision; [[lesson:prog-effort-failure|the effort lesson]] explains how hard to train.

blocks.title: Effort is not a pain instruction
blocks.text: A demanding rep can feel hard without sharp pain. Stop for sharp pain, dizziness or loss of control. Get help with an unfamiliar setup, and see [[lesson:start-safety|training safety]] before practising unsupported lifts.

blocks.title: Practise the checklist with a supported movement

takeaways: Prepare your setup and stopping plan before lifting.
During the rep, prioritise a repeatable path, comfortable range and control.
After the set, log your effort and the cue that helped.

quiz.q: Your final repetitions need a big body swing. What should you do?
options: End the set and reassess the load.
Keep swinging until the planned count is reached.
Shorten the movement and keep the same count.
quiz.why: The goal is clean, repeatable repetitions, not completing a number by changing the exercise.

quiz.q: You keep forgetting a long list of cues during a set. What is a useful change?
options: Repeat the whole list faster during each repetition.
Choose a simple cue after practising the setup.
Change grip and foot position throughout the set.
quiz.why: Prepare details before moving. A simple movement cue leaves less to juggle during the rep.

sources.label: ACSM (2009) — Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults
Helms et al. (2016) — Application of the repetitions in reserve-based rating of perceived exertion scale
A systematic review of attentional focus strategies in weightlifting (2019)

lessons.title: The six movement patterns
lessons.summary: Squat, hinge, push, pull, lunge and carry are useful labels for learning movements. They are a teaching map, not an exhaustive anatomy rule.

blocks.text: After this lesson, you can sort common exercises into squat, hinge, push, pull, lunge and carry patterns. These labels make the exercise library easier to read; they are a coaching map, not six exclusive anatomy boxes.

labels: Squat: knees and hips bend together
Hinge: hips push back, shins stay nearly vertical
blocks.caption: Watch the knees and hips. In the squat they bend together; in the hinge the hips travel back while the shins stay quieter.

items: **Squat:** bend your knees and hips to lower, then stand. Picture sitting down and getting up. Try [[ex:dumbbell-goblet-squat|a goblet squat]].
**Hinge:** send your hips back, with some knee bend, then bring them forward. Picture closing a door behind you with your hips. Try [[ex:dumbbell-romanian-deadlift|a dumbbell Romanian deadlift]].
**Push:** move resistance away from you. [[ex:chest-press-machine|A machine chest press]] is a horizontal push; [[ex:shoulder-press-machine|a shoulder press]] pushes overhead.
**Pull:** draw resistance towards you. [[ex:seated-row-machine|A seated row]] pulls horizontally; [[ex:lat-pulldown|a pulldown]] brings resistance down from overhead.
**Lunge:** use a staggered stance or a stepping movement. [[ex:reverse-lunges|Reverse lunges]] challenge each leg with different support than a squat.
**Carry:** hold a manageable load and walk while staying steady. Think grocery bags, without racing or letting them pull you sideways.

params.prompt: Tap a highlighted region to connect movement patterns with muscles.

blocks.caption: These regions illustrate common contributors, not the only muscles working. A pattern names the movement; the atlas names parts helping you do it.

blocks.text: Squats involve both hips and knees. Hinges put more emphasis on hip movement. Your front thigh muscles help straighten your knees; your buttocks and back-of-thigh muscles help move your hips. Those actions overlap across exercises. You do not switch off your thighs by calling something a hinge.

left.title: Recognise the pattern ✓
items: Watch which joints move and where the resistance travels.
Practise a hinge by moving your hips back with a light load.
Treat balance and a clear walking route as part of a carry.

right.title: Avoid rigid labels ✕
items: Calling every lower-body exercise a squat.
Assuming one pattern trains only one muscle.
Forcing a movement into a category when it combines several.

blocks.text: Not everything fits neatly. [[ex:leg-extension-machine|Leg extensions]] mainly move the knee; [[ex:bicep-curl-dumbbell|curls]] mainly move the elbow. They remain useful exercises even without a perfect pattern label. A [[compound exercise]] moves several joints; an [[isolation exercise]] mainly targets movement at one joint. Both can belong in training.

blocks.title: Sort your next workout
blocks.text: Name the main pattern beside each exercise, then open its guide. If you cannot explain the difference between a squat and hinge, practise unloaded movements with a coach. Understanding a label is not a substitute for learning the actual lift.

For exercise choices and muscle-specific cues, visit [[lesson:part-quads|quads]], [[lesson:part-glutes-hamstrings|glutes and hamstrings]], [[lesson:part-chest|chest]] or [[lesson:part-back|back]]. For arranging them into a week, visit [[lesson:prog-frequency-splits|training schedules]]. This map helps you read a workout; it does not mean every session needs every pattern.

blocks.title: Compare the main patterns

takeaways: Use movement patterns as a learning map, not rigid rules.
Squats bend hips and knees; hinges emphasise moving the hips back.
Different patterns share muscles, and useful exercises can sit outside these labels.

quiz.q: A new exercise sends your hips back with only some knee bend. Which label fits best?
options: A squat because every leg movement is a squat.
A carry because the load stays near the body.
A hinge because hip movement leads the action.
quiz.why: A hinge emphasises moving at the hips. Some knee bend is normal.

quiz.q: A curl does not fit neatly into your six-pattern checklist. What does that mean?
options: The checklist is a shortcut, not a complete system.
Treat the curl as a pull because the weight moves toward you.
Remove it because only six-pattern exercises are useful.
quiz.why: Single-joint exercises can be useful without fitting neatly into this coaching taxonomy.

sources.label: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Appendicular muscles of the pelvic girdle and lower limbs
ACSM (2009) — Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults

lessons.title: Breathing and bracing
lessons.summary: Tighten around your middle to make a steady base. For light work, breathe continuously; heavy-lift breath holding needs individual safety guidance.

blocks.text: After this lesson, you can create a [[brace]] and choose when to breathe during light or demanding work. Think of firming a cylinder around your trunk, not sucking your stomach flat.

‘360-degree bracing’ is a coaching phrase: think front, sides and back of your waist. It is not a measured requirement to expand equally everywhere. Take a comfortable breath, then tighten around your middle as though expecting a gentle bump. Keep your ribs and pelvis comfortably aligned rather than forcing an exaggerated arch.

blocks.title: How to Properly BRACE Your Core
blocks.why: Watch: Squat University demonstrates a practical core brace for lifting.

items.title: Feel the cylinder
items.text: Stand comfortably and place your hands on the sides of your waist. Breathe without lifting your shoulders towards your ears.

items.title: Firm it up
items.text: Gently tighten the front and sides of your middle. You should feel muscle tension, not a demand to suck everything inward.

items.title: Keep breathing on light practice
items.text: Hold that gentle tension while breathing normally. Then try an unloaded movement without losing your balance.

items.title: Use it with an easy load
items.text: For light lifting, breathe in during the easier return and out during the effort. Keep enough trunk tension to stay steady.

groups.title: Before loading
items: I can make my middle firm without sucking it in.
I can keep breathing while holding a gentle brace.
I have checked whether breath holding is appropriate for me.

groups.title: During light practice
items: My support and balance stay steady.
I am not holding one breath across the whole set.
I can return the load safely if I feel unwell.

blocks.caption: Rehearse with an easy load before treating bracing as a heavy-lift skill. This checklist is a coaching aid, not a medical test.

blocks.text: A [[Valsalva manoeuvre]] means trying to breathe out against a closed airway. During demanding lifting, this raises pressure inside your abdomen and may help trunk stiffness. It also raises blood pressure. The pressure effect is real; a promise that it prevents injury is not established by the review.

blocks.title: Check before using breath holds
blocks.text: If you have high blood pressure, a heart or blood-vessel condition, or a medical restriction, ask your doctor about lifting and breath holding. Do not copy heavy-lift breathing advice automatically. Stop for dizziness, faintness or chest pain; chest pain or fainting needs urgent medical attention.

For a healthy lifter learning heavier lifts, a coach may teach a brief breath hold through the demanding part, followed by a reset. That is different from holding your breath through an entire set. Beginners can start with manageable loads and continuous breathing rather than making prolonged breath holds their default.

left.title: Steady base ✓
items: Firm your trunk before starting the movement.
Exhale during the effort on light exercises.
Reset your breathing when the weight is supported safely.

right.title: Avoid ✕
items: Sucking your stomach in and calling that a brace.
Holding your breath through the entire set.
Assuming more pressure guarantees a safer lift.

blocks.text: Bracing is not the same as bending your trunk in [[ex:crunch|a crunch]]. See [[lesson:part-core|core training]] for that distinction. You do not need maximum tension for every tiny movement. Match the preparation to the task, and use [[lesson:tech-what-to-think|the rep checklist]] to make it repeatable.

takeaways: Brace by tightening around your middle, not sucking your stomach in.
For light work, keep breathing and exhale during the effort.
Breath holding raises blood pressure; ask your doctor if you have relevant health conditions.

quiz.q: You are learning a light machine exercise. Which breathing approach fits?
options: Hold one deep breath until every repetition is done.
Breathe continuously and exhale during the effort.
Relax all trunk tension whenever the load moves.
quiz.why: Light practice usually does not require deliberate breath holding. Gentle tension and continuous breathing can coexist.

quiz.q: You have high blood pressure and see heavy-lift breath-holding advice. What comes first?
options: Copy it because pressure always protects the spine.
Use longer holds to make the technique more stable.
Ask your doctor about lifting and breath holding.
quiz.why: The manoeuvre increases blood pressure. Your medical circumstances matter more than a generic lifting cue.

sources.label: Hackett and Chow (2013) — The Valsalva maneuver: intra-abdominal pressure and safety issues during resistance exercise

lessons.title: Range of motion and the stretch
lessons.summary: Use a comfortable, controlled full movement as your starting point. Longer-muscle-length training looks promising, but deeper is not automatically better or safer.

blocks.text: After this lesson, you can choose a controlled, repeatable [[range of motion]] instead of chasing the deepest or heaviest-looking rep. Think of opening a drawer properly rather than rattling its handle.

For a beginner, a comfortable, controlled full range is a useful default. ‘Full’ means the intended movement for that exercise within what you can control. It does not mean forcing every joint to its absolute limit. Your limb lengths, the equipment and your symptoms can change the appropriate endpoint.

blocks.title: Partial Range Of Motion: Broscience Or Legit?
blocks.why: Watch: Jeff Nippard compares full and partial ranges of motion.

stops.title: Shortened-position partial
stops.text: Only the shortened end of the movement. This is not automatically equivalent to practising the complete exercise.

stops.title: Comfortable full range
stops.text: Move through the intended exercise range while staying in control. This is a useful beginner default.

stops.title: Lengthened-position partial
stops.text: Work in the portion where the target muscle is longer. This is a deliberate variation, not bouncing into a painful endpoint.

blocks.caption: The slider compares categories, not depth scores. A longer-muscle-length partial and a shortened-position partial are different training choices.

blocks.title: What range-of-motion reviews found
blocks.text: Reviews generally favour full range for lower-body growth and strength, while upper-body findings are less clear. A newer review found small overall differences and possible benefits from partials at longer muscle lengths. Research is mixed; ‘all partials are useless’ is too strong.

A [[lengthened position]] is where a muscle is relatively stretched during the exercise. In a study by Maeo and colleagues, [[ex:seated-leg-curl-machine|seated leg curls]] produced more hamstring growth than [[ex:lying-leg-curl-machine|lying leg curls]]. This supports interest in longer-muscle-length training, not a rule that every muscle needs extreme stretching.

left.title: Do ✓
items: Choose an endpoint you can control without pain.
Keep that endpoint repeatable when comparing logged sets.
Lower the load if you need it to learn the movement.

right.title: Avoid ✕
items: Bouncing into the bottom to create extra movement.
Shrinking each rep while claiming the same performance.
Treating a stronger stretch sensation as proof of more growth.

blocks.title: Check the bottom with an easy load
blocks.text: Practise [[ex:dumbbell-romanian-deadlift|a dumbbell Romanian deadlift]] using its guide. End the lowering where you can keep the movement controlled. Reaching the floor is not the goal. If you lose your position, shorten the range or reduce the load while learning.

blocks.title: Do not force a painful endpoint
blocks.text: A normal stretch sensation is not permission to push through sharp pain or pinching. Modify the movement and seek qualified help if symptoms persist. Deliberate partial movements can be useful when full range is not currently comfortable.

Once you can repeat a comfortable movement, learn [[lesson:tech-tempo-control|control and tempo]] before adding weight. See [[lesson:part-glutes-hamstrings|hamstring exercise choices]] for muscle-specific options. The goal is a meaningful movement you can reproduce, not winning a depth contest against somebody built differently.

blocks.title: Compare muscle-length positions

takeaways: Start with a comfortable full range you can control.
Longer-muscle-length training is promising, but partial movements are not all equivalent.
Keep your range repeatable, and never force a painful endpoint.

quiz.q: You add weight but your movement becomes much shorter. What is the clearest interpretation?
options: You changed the task, so progress is harder to compare.
You definitely gained strength through the entire movement.
You proved shorter movements always build more muscle.
quiz.why: More weight with a different range is not a like-for-like comparison.

quiz.q: A study favours training at longer muscle lengths. What should you conclude?
options: Every rep must reach the deepest possible joint position.
Controlled longer-position work may help, depending on the exercise.
Any partial movement has the same effect as every other partial.
quiz.why: The muscle, exercise and part of the range matter. The evidence does not justify forcing painful extremes.

sources.label: Schoenfeld and Grgic (2020) — Effects of range of motion on muscle development: systematic review
Pallarés et al. (2021) — Effects of range of motion on resistance training adaptations: systematic review and meta-analysis
Wolf et al. (2023) — Partial vs full range of motion resistance training: systematic review and meta-analysis
Maeo et al. (2021) — Greater hamstrings muscle hypertrophy after training at long versus short muscle lengths

lessons.title: Tempo and control
lessons.summary: Control the lowering and lift smoothly. Tempo notation is a timing instruction, not a secret formula; deliberately ultra-slow repetitions are not automatically better.

blocks.text: After this lesson, you can read tempo notation and control both the working phase and the return. [[Tempo]] is timing, not a secret formula; smooth reps do not need to become slow-motion cinema.

During the working phase, the main target muscle usually shortens as you move against resistance. During the controlled return, it usually lengthens while resisting the load. A pause is a deliberate stop between phases. The return is downward in a curl but upward in a pulldown, so learn the directions for your exercise.

blocks.title: Fast or Slow Reps for Muscle Growth? | Lifting Tempo | Fundamental Series Ep 6
blocks.why: Watch: Jeff Nippard explains lifting tempo and controlled rep speed.

blocks.caption: Practice example: lower for 3 seconds, pause for 1, then lift for 1. This 3-1-1 pattern teaches timing; it is not a proven best growth tempo.

blocks.text: Here, 3-1-1 describes lowering, the bottom pause and lifting, in that order. Some programs use four digits and include a pause at the top. Others write ‘X’ to mean lift with explosive intent. Read your program's definition first. Numbers describe the plan, not a guarantee that every exercise should follow it.

left.title: Control ✓
items: Guide the return without dropping the load.
Keep the same range as the repetition becomes harder.
Let a difficult lifting phase slow naturally while you stay stable.

right.title: Unplanned momentum ✕
items: Bounce out of the bottom because the load is too heavy.
Swing your whole body to start a supposedly strict curl.
Make every phase extremely slow to chase a bigger burn.

blocks.title: What tempo research can say
blocks.text: A review found similar muscle growth across a broad range of repetition durations. Very slow repetitions did not appear better and might be worse, although evidence was limited. Choose timing that lets you practise the intended movement.

blocks.title: Try the timing with a light curl
blocks.text: Use [[ex:bicep-curl-dumbbell|a dumbbell curl]] and start light enough to follow the practice tempo. Keep your elbow movement consistent, guide the return and avoid body swing. If the timing distracts you from control, stop counting and use the cue ‘smooth return’.

Not all fast movement is cheating. Some training intentionally uses speed and power. The issue here is unplanned momentum that changes the exercise you meant to do. On beginner muscle-building exercises, stay repeatable. See [[lesson:tech-range-of-motion|range of motion]] for endpoints and [[lesson:tech-choosing-weight|weight choice]] if control keeps disappearing.

cards.front: Does more burning mean the tempo is better?
cards.back: No. A sensation is not a direct measurement of muscle growth. Judge control and progression over time, not discomfort alone.

cards.front: Must a hard rep match the clock perfectly?
cards.back: No. The lifting phase can slow with effort. Do not speed up with a big swing just to satisfy a timer.

blocks.title: Practise a smooth return

takeaways: Tempo notation tells you how to time the movement; check the program's convention.
Control the lowering without assuming extremely slow repetitions are better.
A hard lifting phase can slow naturally without becoming a bad repetition.

quiz.q: The last lifting phase slows down, but your position and range stay stable. What does that mean?
options: You must swing the load to match the earlier speed.
You must shorten the movement to keep the timer happy.
Slowing with effort is not automatically a mistake.
quiz.why: Control and repeatable technique matter more than matching a precise clock under fatigue.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of this lesson's 3-1-1 practice tempo?
options: To rehearse control and understand the notation.
To guarantee the highest possible muscle growth.
To replace choosing an appropriate training load.
quiz.why: It is a teaching example, not a scientifically established optimum.

sources.label: Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger (2015) — Effect of repetition duration on muscle hypertrophy: systematic review and meta-analysis

lessons.title: Warming up
lessons.summary: Get moving, rehearse the exercise, then gradually approach your working load. A warm-up prepares you to train; it should not become the tiring main event.

blocks.text: After this lesson, you can build a short warm-up that prepares you without tiring you. Rehearse the movement before a demanding set, like a sound check before the concert.

Begin with a few easy minutes of walking or cycling until you feel warmer and ready to move. Then use a [[dynamic warm-up]]: controlled movements related to the exercise. General movement wakes you up; exercise-specific practice checks the positions, equipment and load you are about to use.

blocks.title: How to PROPERLY Warm Up Before Weights
blocks.why: Watch: Jeremy Ethier demonstrates a simple warm-up before lifting weights.

stops.title: General movement
stops.text: Easy walking or cycling. You should feel more ready, not exhausted.

stops.title: Light rehearsal
stops.text: Practise the actual exercise with an easy load. Check the setup, path, breathing and comfortable range.

stops.title: Intermediate load
stops.text: Add some load while keeping the rehearsal easy. Use fewer repetitions as the weight approaches your working load.

stops.title: Near the working load
stops.text: If needed, do a brief, non-tiring rehearsal closer to the planned weight. Rest before your first working set.

blocks.caption: Move through the ramp as a teaching sequence. These stages are not required percentages, and you can skip redundant stages for a light exercise.

items.title: Get generally ready
items.text: Move easily until you feel warm. Avoid turning this into hard cardio before lifting.

items.title: Rehearse the main lift
items.text: Use a light load and check the guide. Adjust the setup now, before the load becomes demanding.

items.title: Approach the working weight
items.text: A practical starting menu is 2–4 ramp-up sets for a demanding first lift. That is coaching guidance, not a proven universal dose. Use fewer if already prepared.

items.title: Rest, then begin training
items.text: Your final rehearsal should not be a struggle. Rest until ready, then start the planned working sets and log those separately.

blocks.text: A review by Fradkin and colleagues found that warming up often improved performance, although protocols varied. Ribeiro and colleagues also found that the warm-up load mattered for squat and bench-press performance. Neither tells us that every beginner needs exactly the same number of warm-up sets or loading percentages.

[[Static stretching]] means holding a stretch. You do not need a long stretching routine before every lift. Prolonged static holds immediately before performance can reduce output; context matters. Brief stretches followed by active movement are different. If a short stretch helps you reach a comfortable position, follow it with movement practice.

left.title: Prepared ✓
items: Your range feels comfortable and your setup is settled.
The rehearsal load moves smoothly without tiring you.
You feel ready for the first working set.

right.title: Overcooked ✕
items: Your warm-up already feels like an all-out workout.
You chase soreness before the planned lifting starts.
You repeat a long ritual without checking whether it helps.

blocks.title: Warm does not mean invincible
blocks.text: A warm-up is not proof that a painful movement is safe, and it cannot guarantee injury prevention. Stop for sharp pain or dizziness. See [[lesson:rec-pain-injury|pain and injury guidance]] if symptoms keep returning.

Later exercises using already-warm muscles may need less preparation, but a new movement or much heavier load still deserves rehearsal. Use [[lesson:tech-what-to-think|the setup checklist]] and read [[lesson:rec-stretching|stretching and flexibility]] for the bigger picture. The best warm-up leaves you ready, not needing recovery from the warm-up.

blocks.title: Easy general movement options

takeaways: Combine easy general movement with light practice of the exercise.
Gradually approach the working load without making warm-up sets exhausting.
Long static stretching is not required, and a warm-up does not guarantee injury prevention.

quiz.q: Your ramp-up sets leave you struggling before the workout begins. What should change?
options: Add more hard rehearsal sets to become better prepared.
Make the rehearsal less tiring and rest before training.
Skip all future warm-ups because preparation never helps.
quiz.why: Preparation should help the working sets, not drain you before they begin.

quiz.q: You are warm, but an exercise still causes sharp pain. What should you do?
options: Stop and reassess instead of forcing the movement.
Continue because warmth proves the movement is safe.
Stretch harder until you can push through the pain.
quiz.why: Feeling warm does not override a pain warning or guarantee that a movement is suitable.

sources.label: Fradkin, Zazryn and Smoliga (2010) — Effects of warming-up on physical performance: systematic review and meta-analysis
Ribeiro et al. (2020) — The role of specific warm-up during bench press and squat exercises
Behm et al. (2016) — Acute effects of stretching on performance, range of motion and injury incidence: systematic review

lessons.title: Choosing the right weight
lessons.summary: Start with a manageable load, compare your clean repetitions with the program's target, and adjust gradually. Effort estimates are useful, not exact measurements.

blocks.text: After this lesson, you can choose a starting weight and adjust it from your reps, technique and [[reps in reserve|RIR]]. The rack has numbers, but your first load is an estimate you refine.

Start with a load you can move comfortably while learning the guide. Rehearse through [[lesson:tech-warm-up|a warm-up ramp]], then perform the repetitions your program asks for. Keep the same path and range. If you cannot control it from the start, choose less weight instead of hoping the set will somehow improve.

[[Reps in reserve]], often shortened to RIR, estimates how many more clean repetitions you could do when you stop. It is the fuel-left-in-the-tank question. Count repetitions with the same technique, not ones you might finish by swinging, shortening the movement or getting help.

blocks.title: How To Estimate Reps In Reserve (ft RP Hypertrophy App)
blocks.why: Watch: Renaissance Periodization explains how to estimate clean reps in reserve.

params.label: How many clean reps were left?

stops.title: 0 RIR: none left
stops.text: You believe another repetition with the same technique was not possible. This is not a target for every set.

stops.title: 1 RIR: one left
stops.text: You estimate one more clean repetition was possible. Do not include repetitions that need a different movement.

stops.title: 2 RIR: two left
stops.text: You estimate two more clean repetitions were possible before you would be unable to continue.

stops.title: 3 RIR: three left
stops.text: You estimate three more clean repetitions were possible. Compare this with the effort your program requests.

stops.title: 4 RIR: four left
stops.text: You estimate four more clean repetitions were possible. This can be useful practice effort, depending on your plan.

stops.title: 5 RIR: five left
stops.text: You estimate five more clean repetitions were possible. When far from your limit, an exact estimate can be harder.

blocks.caption: RIR is a subjective estimate, not a test result. This 0–5 teaching scale shows repetitions left; it is not a separate overall effort-rating scale.

blocks.text: For example, suppose your plan asks for 2 RIR, but you finish with about 4 left. You may need a slightly heavier load next set or next session. If you finish with none left, choose less. These numbers illustrate matching a plan; they do not declare one effort target best for everyone.

left.title: Adjust thoughtfully ✓
items: Compare your estimate with the program's target effort.
Use a small available load change, then reassess.
Keep the same range so your logged performances are comparable.

right.title: Avoid guessing games ✕
items: Copying somebody else's weight because they look similar.
Taking every set to your limit to prove the estimate.
Adding weight while technique keeps becoming less controlled.

blocks.text: Helms and colleagues describe using repetitions left to adjust loads to the lifter's abilities. They also note that estimating effort takes practice. Beginners can be wrong, especially when far from their limit. Treat your estimate as useful feedback rather than a precision instrument. You do not need to perform a maximal test to start.

items.title: Check the set
items.text: Did you finish the planned repetitions with the same comfortable movement? If not, reduce the load or get technique help.

items.title: Check the effort
items.text: Estimate clean repetitions left and compare with your plan. Consider fatigue and readiness today, not just yesterday's number.

items.title: Decide the next move
items.text: If repetitions and effort meet the program's progression rule, increase gradually. Otherwise practise or repeat the load; a stable session still counts.

blocks.text: Stop when another repetition would require losing control, or when pain appears. A slower but steady rep is different from a changed movement. Visit [[lesson:prog-progressive-overload|progression]] for when to increase weight and [[lesson:prog-effort-failure|effort and failure]] for choosing your target. Here, your job is matching that target honestly.

takeaways: Choose a load that allows the planned repetitions with repeatable technique.
Estimate only clean repetitions when judging reps in reserve.
Adjust gradually to match the program, and stop when control or safety is lost.

quiz.q: Your plan requests 2 RIR, but you finish with about 4 clean reps left. What is reasonable?
options: Add a large jump until your technique starts changing.
Force extra repetitions until you cannot move at all.
Try a slightly heavier load and reassess your effort.
quiz.why: A modest adjustment can bring the set closer to the planned effort without making control optional.

quiz.q: You think another rep is possible only with a big swing. Does it count as a clean rep left?
options: Yes, because any way of moving the load is equivalent.
No, because your estimate uses the same technique.
Yes, because the weight remains the same on the rack.
quiz.why: RIR is meaningful only when the imagined extra repetitions keep the movement standard consistent.

sources.label: Helms et al. (2016) — Application of the repetitions in reserve-based rating of perceived exertion scale
ACSM (2009) — Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults

lessons.title: Focus: mind-muscle connection
lessons.summary: Use an outcome cue for demanding movements. Feeling the target muscle may help some simple exercises, but a strong sensation is not proof of growth.

blocks.text: After this lesson, you can choose between an internal cue and an external cue. Zoom in on the working muscle for some isolation work; zoom out to the movement outcome for strength and skill.

[[Internal focus]] means paying attention to your body or a muscle: ‘feel your biceps contract’. [[External focus]] means paying attention to the movement's effect: ‘push the floor away’. Neither lets you bypass learning the setup. The cue should help you perform the exercise, not distract you from balance and control.

blocks.title: How To Use The Mind-Muscle Connection for Growth (What The Science Says)
blocks.why: Watch: Jeff Nippard explains when a mind-muscle cue may help and when it may distract.

params.label: Choose a cue for the task

stops.title: Simple isolation practice
stops.text: On a light curl, try ‘feel the front of your upper arm work’. Keep the actual movement unchanged.

stops.title: Demanding whole-body movement
stops.text: Try an outcome cue such as ‘push the floor away’. Keep detailed setup decisions before the set.

stops.title: The cue is not helping
stops.text: Return to a simple movement instruction or reduce the load. You do not need to chase a sensation to perform useful training.

blocks.caption: These are coaching examples, not rankings of growth. Keep the cue that improves control and discard one that makes the movement worse.

blocks.text: A systematic review of lifting studies found that external focus often helped performance and movement efficiency. That makes outcome cues a useful starting point when strength and skill matter. It does not mean every internal cue is harmful. The exercise, your experience and the exact words can change what helps.

blocks.title: Where internal focus helped
blocks.text: In a study of untrained college-aged men, focusing on the working muscle improved elbow-flexor growth, but not thigh-muscle growth. That suggests a possible benefit in some exercises, not a universal rule.

left.title: Internal cue: zoom in
items: On [[ex:bicep-curl-dumbbell|a dumbbell curl]], notice the front of your upper arm working.
Keep the elbow movement steady rather than chasing a harder squeeze.
Use muscle sensation as feedback, not a measurement of growth.

right.title: External cue: see the task
items: On [[ex:dumbbell-goblet-squat|a goblet squat]], think ‘push the floor away’ as you stand.
On [[ex:chest-press-machine|a machine press]], think ‘push the handles away’.
Let the cue simplify the movement rather than add more mental instructions.

cards.front: If I cannot feel the target muscle, it is not working.
cards.back: Feeling is imperfect feedback. A muscle can contribute without a dramatic sensation. Check the exercise and your movement before chasing a burn.

cards.front: Thinking harder about a muscle guarantees more growth.
cards.back: No. The study found a benefit for elbow-flexor growth, not thigh-muscle growth. A promising finding does not make a universal rule.

cards.front: The best cue works for everybody.
cards.back: No. Try a simple cue, observe the movement, and keep it only if it helps your task.

blocks.title: Compare without changing the exercise
blocks.text: With an easy supported exercise, try an outcome cue during practice. Then try noticing the working muscle. Which makes the movement easier to repeat? Do not change the weight, range and setup at the same time; otherwise you cannot tell what the cue changed.

If sensation keeps taking over, return to [[lesson:tech-what-to-think|the rep checklist]]. For specific muscle cues, visit [[lesson:part-arms|arm training]] or [[lesson:part-chest|chest training]]. For [[hypertrophy|muscle growth]], consistent training and [[lesson:prog-progressive-overload|gradual progression]] matter more than inventing the perfect thought during every repetition.

blocks.title: Practise a cue without chasing a burn

takeaways: External cues often help lifting performance and movement skill.
Internal focus may help some simple exercises, but growth evidence is limited.
Choose cues that improve the movement; feeling a burn does not prove muscle growth.

quiz.q: Thinking about every muscle makes your squat harder to coordinate. What should you try?
options: A simple outcome cue, with setup settled beforehand.
An even longer muscle checklist during every repetition.
Ignoring your setup and only chasing stronger sensations.
quiz.why: An external cue can simplify the task. More conscious detail is not automatically better.

quiz.q: You finish a controlled curl without a dramatic burn. What can you conclude?
options: The muscle definitely received no useful training at all.
The lack of burn does not prove the exercise was ineffective.
The weight must increase until the entire body starts swinging.
quiz.why: Sensation is not a direct measure of the muscle's contribution or future growth.

sources.label: A systematic review of attentional focus strategies in weightlifting (2019)
Schoenfeld et al. (2018) — Differential effects of attentional focus strategies during long-term resistance training

glossary.def: One complete repetition of an exercise movement.
A group of repetitions performed before resting.
Tightening muscles around your trunk to create a steadier base for movement.
How far you move through an exercise or at a joint.
Your estimate of how many more repetitions you could complete with the same technique before being unable to continue.
An exercise involving movement at several joints.
An exercise focused mainly on movement at one joint.
Trying to breathe out against a closed airway, which raises pressure inside your trunk and changes blood pressure.
The part of an exercise where the working muscle is relatively stretched.
The timing of an exercise's lowering, pause and lifting phases.
Holding a position that stretches a muscle rather than moving repeatedly into and out of it.
Controlled movements used to prepare for exercise rather than holding still in a stretch.
Paying attention to a body part or muscle during movement.
Paying attention to the movement's effect, such as pushing a handle away or moving the floor.
An increase in muscle size over time.
